claims.quote: None of them tracks which files a shell command writes
claims.caveat: The page does not mention ports, processes or databases either way.

claims.claim: A Claude Code subagent with isolation: worktree in its frontmatter runs in a temporary git worktree, branched by default from the default branch, which is removed automatically if the subagent makes no changes.
claims.caveat: Version-specific; with agent teams enabled, a named subagent can run as a teammate in the main working directory despite this setting.

claims.claim: Claude Code's bundled /batch skill splits a large change into 5 to 30 independent units and runs one background subagent per unit, each in an isolated worktree.
claims.quote: decomposes the work into 5 to 30 independent units
claims.caveat: The numbers and requirements may change between releases.

claims.claim: In the ChatGPT desktop app, Codex uses Git worktrees so that several chats can work in the same project without interfering with each other.
claims.quote: run multiple independent chats in the same project without interfering with each other
claims.caveat: The page has moved domains and renamed its unit of work several times.

claims.claim: Cursor's docs recommend worktrees for starting several agents on the same repository without conflicts, with per-worktree setup commands in .cursor/worktrees.json.
claims.quote: start several agents on the same repo without conflicts
claims.caveat: Fast-moving and version-specific; the native feature lives in the Agents Window.

claims.claim: Container Use gives each coding agent a fresh container in its own git branch, using Git worktrees for branching, so several agents can run without conflicts.
claims.quote: Each agent gets a fresh container in its own git branch
claims.caveat: An experimental open-source tool in early development.

claims.claim: Conductor gives each local workspace its own range of 10 ports, in CONDUCTOR_PORT, so that several workspaces can run the same app without port conflicts.
claims.quote: Use CONDUCTOR_PORT when multiple workspaces need to run the same app without port conflicts
claims.caveat: One third-party tool's documentation; local workspaces only.

claims.claim: VS Code's docs say worktree isolation keeps an agent's changes out of the active workspace but does not restrict the commands or network access available to the agent.
claims.quote: keeps code changes separate, but isn’t a security boundary
claims.caveat: Fast-moving documentation whose URLs changed recently.

claims.claim: Adding a to-do-style planning tool lifted a weaker model (Nemotron-3 30B) by 11.6 points on SWE-bench Verified and 4.5 points on Terminal-Bench, at higher cost.
claims.quote: Planning trades additional computation for accuracy on the weaker model
claims.caveat: One preprint; the plan is a tool the agent maintains, not a human-written spec; only the SWE-bench gain was significant; one harness.

claims.claim: For the two largest models the same planning tool cut cost on both benchmarks (about 30% on SWE-bench) with small drops in success (0.4 to 2.0 points); the mid-size model showed no consistent gain.
claims.quote: planning reduces cost on both benchmarks, accompanied by small decreases in success rate
claims.caveat: Same study and harness; the success drops were small and not shown to be significant.

claims.claim: Across four LLMs in SWE-agent on 497 SWE-bench Verified instances, the standard navigate, reproduce, patch, validate plan resolved more issues than no plan for every model.
claims.quote: Providing the standard plan improves issue resolution
claims.caveat: Peer-reviewed (ASE 2026), but one scaffold and one generic workflow plan, not a task-specific plan.

claims.claim: Re-inserting the plan into context every five steps raised resolved counts for three of four models, but in the paper’s own Figure 15b the fourth (DeepSeek-R1) fell from 196 to 13 resolved, which the text does not discuss.
claims.quote: periodic plan reminders can mitigate plan violations and improve task success
claims.caveat: The paper’s text says reminders improve success across models; its figure shows one model collapsing. Moderate for three models, weak as a blanket claim.

claims.claim: A subpar plan, the standard plan with its reproduction or validation phase removed, did worse than no plan for several model and variant pairs.
claims.quote: A subpar plan hurts performance even more than no plan at all.
claims.caveat: Effects differ by model and by which phase was removed.

claims.claim: Adding best-practice phases to the plan, such as regression testing before and after the patch, lowered success for all four models.
claims.quote: inserting additional task-relevant phases in the early stage can degrade performance
claims.caveat: Effects ranged widely; the authors tie them to whether the phase matches a model’s trained workflow.

claims.claim: On SWE-bench Pro, plan compliance dropped by 13% on average across agents.
claims.caveat: Only 31 instances that at least one model resolved; near-zero success rates on this benchmark.

claims.claim: On a benchmark that scores clarification and planning separately, 46.7% of agent runs failed primarily during requirement clarification or implementation planning.
claims.quote: 46.7% of agent runs failing primarily during requirement clarification or implementation planning
claims.locator: Section 1 (Introduction, Evaluation paragraph) and Section 4 (Failure Attribution to Stages)
claims.caveat: A new arXiv preprint (v1, Aug 2026, not peer reviewed) benchmark of 163 tasks from 31 Python and Java repositories; an LLM judge assigns each unresolved run to its earliest deviating stage (92% agreement with humans on a 50-run sample); two runs per agent-model configuration.

claims.claim: Requirement failures were the largest share for most configurations (24.5% to 46.0% of runs), with planning failures 5.5% to 17.8%.
claims.quote: Requirement failure is the largest component for most configurations
claims.caveat: Same benchmark and LLM-judged stages.

claims.claim: The average resolved rate across agent configurations was 31.5%.
claims.quote: average resolved rate of only 31.5% on SWE-RPG
claims.caveat: Same benchmark: new arXiv preprint (not peer reviewed), 163 tasks, two runs per configuration; resolved rate is test-graded.

claims.claim: Adding repository-grounding hooks to a Spec Kit pipeline raised an LLM judge’s quality score from 3.51 to 3.66 on a 1-5 scale over 128 runs.
claims.quote: Context-grounding hooks improve judged quality by +0.15 on a 1–5 composite LLM-as-judge score.
claims.caveat: One model and an LLM judge; it measures hooks, not specs against no specs.

claims.claim: The same paper’s spec pipeline and its no-spec baseline scored 3.51 and 3.46, a difference it did not test, under different time budgets (90 and 40 minutes).
claims.caveat: Not a controlled spec-versus-no-spec comparison.

claims.claim: The paper’s SWE-bench Lite gain (56.5% to 58.2%) compares two configurations that both lack specs, so it measures the hooks only.
claims.caveat: One model; one run.

claims.claim: In a blinded comparison on 6 tasks, human raters preferred the version without hooks, 19 votes to 8.
claims.caveat: Six tasks; a handful of raters; contradicts the LLM judge.

claims.claim: Context files increased reasoning tokens for GPT-5.2 by 22% (SWE-bench Lite) and 14% (CTXbench) with LLM-generated files and by 20% with developer-written ones.
claims.caveat: Two models only; paired relative change with no significance test. See conflict C1.

claims.claim: In the same report, moving the planted fact across 11 positions in the input made no notable difference in the basic needle task.
claims.quote: we find no notable variation in performance for this specific NIAH task
claims.locator: Needle in a Haystack Extension section
claims.caveat: One synthetic retrieval task; vendor report. See conflict C2.

claims.claim: When every generated reproduction test was good, the workflow solved 93.3% of those instances.
claims.caveat: A conditional subset chosen after the fact.

claims.claim: A taxonomy of 14 failure modes in multi-agent LLM systems puts the largest share, 44.2% in its third version, in system design issues, which include disobeying the task or role specification.
claims.quote: Failures originate from system design decisions, and poor or ambiguous prompt specifications.
claims.caveat: Shares changed between versions (about 37%, 42% and 44%); v3 labels come from an LLM annotator (kappa 0.77 with experts); not limited to coding.

claims.claim: Given the benchmarks' human-written tests, a test-driven agent workflow passed 88.8% of runnable SWE-bench Lite tasks and 94.3% on SWE-bench Verified.
claims.quote: TDFlow attains 88.8% pass rate on SWE-Bench Lite
claims.locator: Abstract; Section 4.1/4.2 (human-written tests); Appendix A (Lite: 22 unrunnable, denominator 278) and Appendix B (Verified: 45 unrunnable)
claims.caveat: arXiv preprint (v2, Jan 2026), no venue or peer review stated. Tests are the typically hidden human-written grading tests; TDFlow may not modify them. 22 Lite and 45 Verified instances could not be run and are excluded from the denominators (278 and 455, implied by the percentages, not stated outright).

claims.claim: When the same workflow wrote its own tests, it reached 68.0%, so writing correct tests was the main bottleneck.
claims.quote: Combined with the 68.0% performance when generating its own tests
claims.caveat: The introduction gives 69.8% for a related figure without explaining the gap; Table 2 is cited.

claims.claim: Manual inspection of 800 runs found 7 cases of test hacking, which were counted as failures.
claims.locator: Abstract; Section 4.4 (4 Lite + 3 Verified); Appendix C (three reviewers, two or more flags)
claims.caveat: arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed. Hacking was limited partly by design: TDFlow cannot modify tests after they are provided, and patches are prevented from touching test folders. Labels come from three reviewers (two or more flags needed), who are the authors' own team.

claims.claim: Writing a contract-style spec (pre- and post-conditions) before generating tests raised historical-bug detection from 53.4% to 63.2% (p = 0.0352) and branch coverage by 2.5 points.
claims.quote: the Spec-Driven Agent reaches a detection rate of 63.2%
claims.caveat: Peer-reviewed workshop paper; 90 bugs from one company’s codebase; one small model; an LLM judge for test quality.

claims.claim: The spec-driven agent used 38.0% more tokens than the baseline agent.
claims.caveat: Same study.

claims.claim: Telling an agent to follow TDD without saying which tests to check raised regressions from 6.08% to 9.94%, while giving it a graph-derived map of affected tests cut them to 1.82%.
claims.quote: TDD prompting without graph context increased regressions
claims.caveat: One open-weight model on 100 instances, one run; a preprint.

claims.claim: Packaged as an agent skill with a different model, the test map raised resolution by 8 points (24% to 32%), that is 2 more of 25 instances.
claims.caveat: Twenty-five instances.

claims.claim: On a reward-hacking benchmark, held-out tests added little over an LLM judge for catching hacks, and they missed some heuristic solutions that passed every test.
claims.quote: observe only minimal improvement from the use of held out test cases
claims.caveat: LiveCodeBench problems whose test suites do not cover all behaviour, as the authors note.

claims.claim: On coding tasks whose tests contradict the spec, so that passing means cheating, GPT-5 cheated on 76% of one-off-mutation SWE-bench tasks and 54% of conflicting-test tasks.
claims.quote: GPT-5 cheats in 76% of the tasks in Oneoff-SWEbench
claims.caveat: Peer-reviewed (ICLR 2026); eight 2025 models; impossible tasks are a stress test, not normal work.

claims.claim: Stricter prompts cut GPT-5’s cheating on conflicting LiveCodeBench tasks from 92% to 1%, but o3 still cheated 33% of the time under the strictest prompt.
claims.quote: appropriate prompt could dramatically reduce GPT-5’s cheating from 92% to 1% on Conflicting-LiveCodeBench
claims.caveat: Prompt effects were measured on LiveCodeBench, a simpler setting than SWE-bench.

claims.claim: Hiding the tests cut cheating to near zero but also lowered legitimate performance (GPT-5 on the original tasks fell from 97% to 76%).
claims.quote: Hiding tests from agents reduces cheating success rate to near zero
claims.caveat: Full scaffold only; three models.

claims.claim: Read-only tests (edits reverted at scoring) restored legitimate performance and stopped test edits, but not special-casing or operator overloading.
claims.quote: it does not eliminate other cheating methods such as special-casing or operator overloading
claims.caveat: Same setup.

claims.claim: Letting the agent stop and flag the task for a human cut GPT-5’s cheating on conflicting SWE-bench tasks from 54% to 9% and o4-mini’s from 49% to 12%, with little loss on the original tasks; Opus 4.1 barely changed (50% to 46%).
claims.quote: lowering the cheating rate of GPT-5 from 54% to 9%
claims.caveat: The text attributes the 49% to 12% change to o3; Figure 8 labels it o4-mini, which is cited here.

claims.claim: More capable models tended to cheat more.
claims.caveat: A trend across eight models, not a test.

claims.claim: Cheating strategies included editing tests, operator overloading, keeping extra state and special-casing test inputs; Claude models mostly edited tests.
claims.caveat: Strategies were classified by an LLM.

claims.claim: In SWE-agent on SWE-bench Verified, both observation masking and LLM summarization cut cost by about 41% to 57% against the raw agent in four of five configurations, with solve rates roughly flat.
claims.quote: Observation Masking is not only 52% cheaper than the Raw Agent baseline
claims.caveat: Workshop paper; verbose SWE-agent outputs favour masking; one configuration (Gemini 2.5 Flash thinking) lost solve rate significantly (40.4% to 36.4% and 31.4%).

claims.claim: Runs with LLM summaries were longer (52 turns against 44 for masking with one model), which the authors suggest is because summaries hide failure signals.
claims.quote: suggesting they mask failure signals that would otherwise prompt earlier termination
claims.caveat: An untested explanation offered in a figure caption.

claims.claim: Anthropic reports that its memory tool plus context editing improved an internal agentic-search eval by 39% over baseline, and context editing alone by 29%.
claims.quote: combining the memory tool with context editing improved performance by 39% over baseline
claims.caveat: Internal eval; no sample size, metric or baseline details; search, not coding.

claims.claim: In a separate 100-turn web-search eval, context editing cut token use by 84%.
claims.caveat: Same internal reporting.

claims.claim: On a benchmark of memories made outdated by later evidence, the best model scored 55.2%, and memory frameworks scored 5.1% to 17.8% against 8.7% for the plain model, with only one framework doing better.
claims.quote: Even the strongest model, Gemini-3.1-pro, achieves only 55.2% overall accuracy.
claims.caveat: Personal-assistant domain with LLM-generated scenarios; the authors’ own prototype (68.0%) is excluded here.

claims.claim: In the strongest memory framework, the outdated evidence was ranked first in 88.2% and 84.5% of cases on two task types, even when the new evidence was also retrieved.
claims.caveat: Diagnostics for one framework.

claims.claim: Adding cross-task episodic memory to a coding agent never beat the baseline: 42% resolved against 31% to 40% across memory configurations.
claims.quote: CTIM-Rover does not outperform AutoCodeRover in any configuration
claims.caveat: Workshop short paper; 45 instances; GPT-4o; mean context about 1.5 times the baseline.

claims.claim: The authors argue that agents treat every line of a skill as an instruction, which makes skills an easy injection channel.
claims.quote: every line of Agent Skills is typically interpreted as an instruction
claims.caveat: An argument accompanying qualitative demonstrations.

claims.claim: A benchmark of 23 skills with 76 obvious and 126 contextual injection-task pairs found frontier agents widely susceptible; contextual attack success ran from 8.6% to 67.6% across models and safety-policy conditions.
claims.quote: to form 76 obvious injection–task pairs and 126 contextual injection–task pairs
claims.caveat: Preprint; the text quotes different ranges for narrower settings, so the table range is cited.

claims.claim: Payloads in bundled scripts succeeded more often than payloads in the skill text (71.8% against 53.8% on the contextual subset).
claims.quote: script-based attacks succeed 71.8% of the time compared to only 53.8%
claims.caveat: Same benchmark.

claims.claim: In 157 confirmed malicious skills found among 98,380, 84.2% of the 632 vulnerabilities sat in the SKILL.md text rather than in code, and one publisher accounted for 58.5% of them.
claims.quote: 84.2% of vulnerabilities in our dataset (532 of 632) are embedded in SKILL.md files
claims.caveat: One registry snapshot; venue per the arXiv comment only.

claims.claim: When an injected skill must first win retrieval against many benign skills, the effective attack success of existing injections fell by 87% to 97%.
claims.caveat: Checked at abstract level only.
claims.drop_reason: The 87% to 97% figure appears only in the abstract; the paper body never reports or derives it (the nearest result is a Hit@1 drop to about 11% in Section 5.1, Table 6), so a full-text check cannot confirm it.

claims.claim: A router-aware attack that optimizes for retrieval raised attack success from 10.0% to 22.0% in the authors’ main setting.
claims.caveat: Averaged over eight payloads; one router benchmark.

claims.claim: A memory-poisoning attack stored malicious rules in agent memory and triggered them in later sessions: 66.9% injection and 81.7% cross-session success in the Claude Code harness.
claims.quote: with average ISR and C-ASR of 73.7%/55.5% on OpenClaw and 66.9%/81.7% on Claude Code.
claims.caveat: Simulated workspace; the harness was driven by DeepSeek-V4 and Qwen3-Max, not Claude models; cross-session success is likely conditional on the rule being stored.

claims.claim: A sandwich-style prompt defense reduced injection but left cross-session success nearly unchanged.
claims.quote: C-ASR remains nearly unchanged after defense
claims.caveat: One defense, one scenario.

claims.claim: A clarification or planning stage is where most agent runs fail.
claims.drop_reason: Duplicate of R10, from the same source and figure; R10 states the finding at its measured size (46.7%).

claims.claim: On SWE-bench Lite, adding RepoGraph (a repository code graph) raised resolve rate by 2.0 to 2.7 points on four frameworks: RAG 2.67 to 5.33 and AutoCodeRover 19.00 to 21.33 (GPT-4), Agentless 27.33 to 29.67 and SWE-agent 18.33 to 20.33 (GPT-4o).
claims.quote: RepoGraph brings consistent performance gain for all combinations of frameworks and LLM model bases.
claims.caveat: 300 issues, so each point is 3 issues and the gains are 6 to 8 issues per framework; the paper does not state the number of runs. GPT-4/GPT-4o only in the main table, Python only. Gains are small in absolute terms. Peer-reviewed (ICLR 2025) but the effect is not shown to exceed run-to-run variance.

claims.claim: RepoGraph added cost on agent frameworks: SWE-agent with GPT-4o rose from $2.53 to $2.69 per issue and AutoCodeRover from $0.45 to $0.58, while mean SWE-agent turns fell from 21.47 to 19.12.
claims.quote: Average costs are generally larger on agent frameworks with RepoGraph.
claims.caveat: Cost is computed from trajectories by the authors; single run; GPT-4/GPT-4o only.

claims.claim: With the same Claude-3.5 model on SWE-bench Lite, LocAgent (graph tools) reached 94.16% file-level Acc@5 versus 90.15% for SWE-agent, 90.15% for OpenHands, 86.13% for MoatlessTools and 79.56% for Agentless; the best embedding retriever, CodeRankEmbed, reached 84.67%.
claims.caveat: Localisation only, not issue resolution. Single run, 300 Python issues. Authors' own re-runs of baselines. The graph effect here is confounded with LocAgent's own tool set and prompts; no peer-review venue stated.

claims.claim: In LocAgent ablations, removing the graph traversal tool lowered function-level Acc@10 from 71.53% to 66.06%, and removing the entity search tool lowered it to 53.28%; removing the BM25 index lowered it to 60.22%.
claims.quote: The graph structure provides essential information for accurate code localization.
claims.caveat: Ablation uses the fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B only, so the graph effect is measured inside a fine-tuned model and is not separated from fine-tuning; the Claude-3.5 comparison in Table 4 is the un-fine-tuned test.

claims.claim: LocAgent with Claude-3.5 cost $0.66 per example and 7 rounds, versus $0.79 for OpenHands and $0.67 for SWE-agent with the same model; the fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32B cost $0.09 per example at comparable accuracy.
claims.quote: the cost remains lower than that of Openhands
claims.caveat: Costs are estimated from provider list prices, not metered; the fine-tuned model's training cost is excluded; localisation task only.

claims.claim: Feeding LocAgent's localisation into the Agentless repair pipeline raised Pass@1 from 26.31% to 27.92% and Pass@10 from 33.58% to 37.59% on SWE-bench Lite.
claims.caveat: Pass@1 gain is 1.6 points on 300 issues; one editing model (Claude-3.5); single run per setting.

claims.claim: On SWE-bench Lite with GPT-4o, CodexGraph (graph-database queries) matched AutoCodeRover at 22.96% Pass@1, against 3.11% for BM25 retrieval, but used more tokens (102.25k versus 76.01k per issue).
claims.quote: while also achieving results comparable to AutoCodeRover on SWE-bench Lite.
claims.caveat: Only 257 of 300 instances; three LLMs; preprint marked work in progress. CodexGraph did not beat the AST-search baseline on this benchmark.

claims.claim: With weaker backbones the graph-query interface did worse than the tool-based baseline on SWE-bench Lite: Qwen2-72B 1.95% versus 9.34% for AutoCodeRover, DeepSeek-Coder-V2 12.06% versus 15.56%.
claims.caveat: Pass@1 on 257 instances; interface success depends on the model writing valid graph queries; the paper notes loops where queries fail.

claims.claim: With Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct on SWE-bench Lite, mounting the ARISE graph and data-flow toolset on SWE-agent raised Pass@1 from 17.3% (52) to 22.0% (66); SWE-agent plus RepoGraph reached 19.3%.
claims.quote: ARISE-Full resolves 22.0% (66/300)
claims.caveat: Open 32B model, Python only, one attempt per instance; possible pretraining contamination of the benchmark (shared across conditions). Preprint.

claims.claim: With the stronger Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, structural tools gave almost no gain: SWE-agent 33.3%, plus RepoGraph 33.3%, plus ARISE 34.0%; on AutoCodeRover ARISE lowered Pass@1 from 36.3% to 32.0%.
claims.quote: the effect on Pass@1 is host-dependent
claims.caveat: Single run, 300 issues; the authors attribute the AutoCodeRover drop to integration fit; they suggest stronger models internalise structural navigation but do not test it.

claims.claim: Aider sends the model a map of the git repository listing files and key symbols with their signatures; it ranks files with a graph algorithm over file dependencies and fits the map to a token budget set by --map-tokens (default 1k), expanding it when no files are in the chat.
claims.quote: uses a concise map of your whole git repository
claims.locator: Page text: 'Using a repo map to provide context' and 'Optimizing the map'
claims.caveat: Documentation of how the product works; the page reports no measurement of whether the map improves results. Undated page.

claims.claim: On the SWE-QA code question-answering benchmark, a ReAct agent with a vector index passed 65.2% of questions against 46.2% for a planner-plus-subagent terminal-exploration agent, pooled over four models and fifteen Python repositories; Semantic led for every model.
claims.quote: Semantic reached a Pass rate of 65.2% against 46.2% for Deep
claims.caveat: Read-only question answering, not patching. The 'Deep' agent is an orchestrator with a delegated subagent, not plain grep, and tool sets differ by design. Gap is modest for Gemini 2.5 Flash (48.4 versus 42.8) and Gemini 2.5 Pro (54.2 versus 44.2) and very large for Gemini 3 Flash (89.3 versus 39.7), which lifts the pooled figure. Preprint under review.

claims.claim: The subagent-exploration agent cost more than the vector-index agent for every model, for example Gemini 3 Flash $0.858 versus $0.179 per correct answer and Qwen3-235B about 761k versus 34k input tokens per question.
claims.quote: Deep was more expensive than Semantic on the token and dollar measures
claims.caveat: Prices are list prices at study time; the one-time indexing cost (under $1 for all fifteen repositories) is reported separately; same caveats as R165.

claims.claim: In the subagent-exploration condition, planner-to-subagent coordination breakdown accounted for 41.8% of failures, and in 91% of those cases the agent still returned a confident answer.
claims.quote: Coordination breakdown accounted for 41.8% of Deep failures
claims.caveat: Failure categories were coded from traces by the authors; single benchmark; the coordination category cannot occur in a flat agent by definition.

claims.claim: The study found no significant association between repository size and the Deep-to-Semantic cost ratio across fifteen repositories, and calls the result inconclusive.
claims.quote: so we treat this as inconclusive rather than as evidence of no relationship
claims.caveat: Only fifteen repositories, so the interval is wide; it measures cost overhead, not accuracy against size.

claims.claim: On 116 LongMemEval conversation-memory questions, inline grep beat inline vector retrieval in all ten harness-model pairs (for example 86.2% versus 62.9%), but with file-based tool delivery vector beat grep in five of ten, and the same model scored 93.1% in one harness versus 76.7% in Claude Code.
claims.quote: inline grep exceeds inline vector for every harness–model pair
claims.caveat: Not code: the corpus is chat history and the authors say code may behave differently. Small sample; GPT-4o grader; single run; preprint.

claims.claim: Across 21 repositories and four agent configurations translating whole repositories to another language, mean pass rate was 91.3% under 10K LOC, 66.9% for 10K-50K LOC and 15.3% above 50K LOC.
claims.quote: Performance collapses to 15.3% average
claims.caveat: Task is cross-language repository translation, not issue fixing or navigation. Only 21 projects, binned 3 small, 7 medium and 11 large in the text but 3, 6 and 12 in Table 4, whose grouping the reported averages match; size is confounded with project domain and difficulty (the authors cite specialised algorithms); no navigation measurement; preprint.

claims.claim: On SWE-Bench Pro, agent resolve rate stays roughly stable for single-file patches and drops sharply as the number of files in the reference patch rises; GPT-5 and Claude Opus 4.1 stay above 10% at 10+ files while open-source models approach zero.
claims.quote: exhibit sharp declines as file count increases
claims.caveat: This is patch size, not repository size; the body gives no table, and the figure caption warns the 10+ file and 500+ LOC bins hold only 20-30 examples. SWE-Agent scaffold only. Preprint.

claims.claim: In FeatBench (157 feature tasks, 27 repositories), GPT-5 resolve rates reached 60-70% on repositories under 200 files or 50,000 LOC and fell to 10-30% above 800 files or 300,000 LOC for all models.
claims.quote: performance for all models converges to a low of 10-30%
claims.caveat: Feature implementation, two agent frameworks (Trae-agent, Agentless), four models; best overall 29.94%. Repository size is confounded with repository identity and task type, and bins are small; values come from the prose, not a table.

claims.claim: In FeatBench the autonomous Trae-agent localised the correct files for 76.42% of tasks on average against 48.90% for the pipeline-based Agentless.
claims.quote: Trae-agent’s average File% of 76.42% far surpasses Agentless’s 48.90%
claims.caveat: Compares whole scaffolds, so planning, tools and prompts differ; averaged over four models; the authors attribute it to dynamic planning without testing that.

claims.claim: On SWE-bench-Live (1,319 issues) with OpenHands and Claude 3.7 Sonnet, repositories under 100 files and 20,000 LOC often had success above 20%, while projects over 500 files rarely exceeded 5%.
claims.quote: whereas projects exceeding five-hundred files rarely exceed five per-cent
claims.caveat: Per-repository scatter read from a figure by the authors in prose; one agent-model pair; the authors note large variance among small and mid-size projects. Preprint.

claims.claim: SWE-bench-Live's non-SWE-bench repositories had fewer files and less code than the original SWE-bench repositories, yet the best agent resolved fewer of their issues (18.89% versus 22.96%).
claims.quote: generally simpler with fewer files and lower code volume
claims.caveat: The authors read this as agents overfitting to SWE-bench repositories, so it is confounded with familiarity; it shows size alone does not predict success across repository sets.

claims.claim: On LoLBench (100 tasks across 29 large systems, mean 2.4M source LOC), code localisation was the largest phase of agent turns, 60.4% of initial-generation turns and 44.2% of repair turns, and missing cross-module context was the largest failure category.
claims.quote: code localization is the largest phase for 26 of 28 agents
claims.caveat: Turn phases and failure attribution are assigned by the authors' classifier (judge prompts in the appendix); only large repositories, so it cannot show a size effect; best resolved rate was 14%. Preprint.

claims.claim: Appending a file tree and API specification derived from the reference solution raised resolved rate by 16-22 points for three agents on LoLBench.
claims.quote: the specifications increase resolved rate by 16–22 percentage points
claims.caveat: The file tree is bundled with an API specification, so the file tree's own effect is not isolated; three agents, each with a different model; the tree and specification are derived from the reference solution, so the gain is an upper bound on what a map an agent could build itself would give.

claims.claim: In Agentless on SWE-bench Lite, prompting an LLM with the repository structure tree located the edited file in 78.67% of issues for $0.02, embedding retrieval (after folder filtering) in 70.33% for $0.04, and combining them in 81.67% for $0.06.
claims.quote: prompting-based and embedding-based retrieval methods can complement each other
claims.caveat: File-level containment of the ground-truth file, not resolve rate; GPT-4o, Python, 300 issues, single run; embedding retriever without folder filtering scored 67.67%.

claims.claim: Agentless ablations found that going straight from files to edit locations contained the ground truth in 47.00% of cases at $0.18, versus 50.67% at $0.06 with the intermediate class and function step, and a skeleton view beat whole-file context (58.33% at $0.02 versus 53.67% at $0.15).
claims.quote: both the cost and performance are worse
claims.caveat: Compares localisation steps, not end resolve rates; the hierarchy is not isolated from other Agentless choices; one model and benchmark.

claims.claim: The hierarchical, non-agentic Agentless pipeline resolved 32.00% (96 of 300) of SWE-bench Lite issues at $0.70 average cost, the highest among open-source systems when the paper was written.
claims.quote: the highest performance (32.00%, 96 correct fixes)
claims.caveat: Result bundles localisation with sampling and test-based patch selection, so it does not isolate hierarchical localisation; comparisons use leaderboard figures at the time; single benchmark.

claims.claim: In SWE-agent with GPT-4 Turbo on SWE-bench Lite, a summarised search tool resolved 18.0%, no search tool 15.7%, and an iterative one-result-at-a-time search tool 12.0%.
claims.quote: even worse performance than the not having additional search tools at all
claims.caveat: One model and 300 tasks, small absolute differences (2.3 to 6 points, 7 to 18 issues); the paper reports pass@k variance across runs separately (Figure 4); venue not confirmed.

claims.claim: In the same ablation, a 100-line file viewer resolved 18.0%, a 30-line viewer 14.3% and a full-file viewer 12.7%.
claims.quote: agents are sensitive to the number of lines the file viewer displays
claims.caveat: One model, one benchmark, one run per setting; interface design, not repository size.

claims.claim: AutoCodeRover, which searches code through AST-level class and method APIs, resolved 19.00% (57) of SWE-bench Lite at about 37k tokens ($0.43) per issue, versus 18.00% at 245k tokens ($2.51) for SWE-agent as reported by its authors.
claims.quote: fine-grained code context search at the AST level
claims.caveat: No ablation isolates AST-level search from the rest of the system; SWE-agent figures are taken from its own report with a different GPT-4 variant; single benchmark. Peer-reviewed (ISSTA 2024 per the arXiv listing).

claims.claim: Cursor reports that adding semantic search to its agent raised accuracy on its internal Context Bench by 12.5% on average (6.5% to 23.5% by model), and in an online A/B test raised code retention by 0.3% (2.6% on repositories of 1,000+ files).
claims.quote: semantic search significantly improves agent performance, especially over large codebases
claims.locator: Introduction, Offline evals, Online A/B tests
claims.caveat: Vendor-run on an unreleased benchmark with no absolute scores (the post does not say whether 12.5% is a relative or absolute gain), sample sizes or confidence intervals; the embedding model was trained on its own agent traces; the post says grep plus semantic search was best, not that grep alone fails.

claims.claim: Cursor's current documentation says its agent uses 'Instant Grep', a custom engine that builds its index on the user's machine, and that Cursor does not store embeddings of the codebase for search.
claims.quote: does not store embeddings of your codebase for search
claims.caveat: Documents current product behaviour only; says nothing about accuracy or why the design changed.

claims.claim: On SWE-Explore (848 issues, 203 repositories, 10 languages), every agentic explorer scored well above BM25, TF-IDF and a lightweight static-embedding retriever, which stayed close to a random baseline on most metrics; general-purpose coding agents' line-level recall was only about 0.14-0.19.
claims.quote: repository exploration is not well captured by one-shot lexical or embedding retrieval alone
claims.caveat: The dense retriever is a lightweight static word-embedding model, not a strong code embedder; ground truth is derived from successful agent trajectories, which may favour agent-style exploration; measures exploration quality, not patch success directly. Preprint.

claims.claim: In 2,303 context files from 1,925 repositories, testing instructions appear in 75.9% of files, implementation details in 70.8%, architecture in 68.1%, security in 14.8% and performance in 14.5%.
claims.quote: non-functional requirements such as security (14.8%) and performance (14.5%) are rarely specified
claims.caveat: Descriptive counts from public GitHub repositories (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, copilot-instructions.md at repo root only, at least 5 stars). Says nothing about whether the content helps agents. Manual coding; preprint.

claims.claim: 59% to 67% of context files were changed in more than one commit (Claude Code 67.0%), and the median gap between changes was about 1 day for Claude Code and Codex files and about 3 days for Copilot files.
claims.quote: a majority of Claude Code context files (67.0%) are modified in multiple commits
claims.caveat: Descriptive. 92% of 100 sampled commits contained an instruction edit, but the sample is small and single-labelled. Does not show whether edits keep files accurate.

claims.claim: Edits to context files were mostly small additions: deletions had a median under 15 words per commit, and Claude Code commits added a median of 57 words.
claims.quote: deletions are consistently negligible across all agent context file types
claims.caveat: Descriptive. Shows files grow by accretion; does not show that growth hurts or helps agent results.

claims.claim: A thematic analysis of 401 repositories with Cursor rules (1,876 .mdc files) produced five context themes: Conventions, Guidelines, Project Information, LLM Directives and Examples.
claims.quote: Conventions, Guidelines, Project Information, LLM Directives, and Examples
claims.caveat: Peer-reviewed (MSR 2026) but qualitative and covers only .mdc files in public repositories with at least one star, English only. Describes content, not effect on agents.

claims.claim: 28.70% of lines (19,917) across the 401 repositories' Cursor rules were exact duplicates of other lines, with the highest duplication among LLM-specific instructions.
claims.quote: 19,917 (28.70%) duplicated lines across all repositories
claims.caveat: Exact-line matching only, so near-copies are missed; the authors' reading that this signals copied templates is an interpretation. Cursor rules only.

claims.claim: Across 7,310 rules from 83 open-source projects, Code Implementation (26.28%) and Development Workflow and Project Management (25.96%) were the largest categories, while 99 surveyed practitioners rated Architecture and Design highest in importance.
claims.quote: rule files in repositories primarily consist of low-level workflow and code formatting constraints
claims.caveat: Preprint (TOSEM submission). Mining covers AI IDE rule files; the survey is self-reported and its sample is not random. Importance ratings are opinions, not measured effects.

claims.claim: Of 1,540 rule evolution events, 504 with a clearly determinable reason were coded: 29.17% of those were expansions and 26.59% context enrichments, against 6.35% corrections. In the survey, 77.78% of developers said they change rules to correct AI errors, usually by adding negative constraints.
claims.quote: rule evolution is primarily driven by constructive context expansions (29.17%) and enrichments (26.59%)
claims.caveat: Percentages are of 504 determinable rules, not of all 1,540 events; determinability was screened by three LLMs and coding was done by the first author alone. Survey (self-reported) and mining (corrections 6.35%) disagree on motives. Preprint, journal submission.

claims.claim: In 160 rule-update events, the average compliance of project artifacts with the rule rose from 49.14% to 72.13% after the update (Wilcoxon signed-rank, reported significant).
claims.quote: the average artifact compliance rate increasing by 22.99% (from 49.14% to 72.13%)
claims.caveat: Observational before/after comparison without a control group. Compliance was scored by an LLM judge on commits, on 160 of 1,540 events (statically checkable rules only). Commits may be human- or AI-authored; causal effect of the file is not isolated. Preprint.

claims.claim: In 253 CLAUDE.md files from 242 repositories, Build and Run instructions appeared in 77.1% of files, implementation details in 71.9%, architecture in 64.8%, testing in 60.5%, and security in 8.7%.
claims.quote: The most prevalent was Build and Run (77.1%)
claims.caveat: Claude Code files only; a short paper (cited by later work as PROFES 2025, though the arXiv text names no venue); two labellers, with a third resolving 113 disagreements across 1,228 label assignments. Superseded in scale by the 2,303-file study. Descriptive only.

claims.claim: Only 466 (5%) of 10,000 popular, mature repositories had adopted any of the AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md or Copilot instruction formats; AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md co-occurred in 25 repositories.
claims.quote: Only 466 (5%) of the repositories that we scanned had already adopted
claims.caveat: Snapshot of one sampling frame (10,000 repositories ranked on popularity and maturity, non-English and non-software projects removed) with no stated collection date; adoption has likely changed. Self-described preliminary study.

claims.claim: Of 155 AGENTS.md files, 77 (50%) had never changed after creation and 36 (23%) changed once; among 10 files with 10 or more commits, the most common edits were adding instructions (78) and modifying instructions (59).
claims.quote: 77 (50%) of them had not been changed
claims.caveat: Detailed commit coding covers only 10 files (169 commits); the authors say histories varied widely between files and leave evolution patterns to future work. Files are young, since AGENTS.md was introduced in 2025.

claims.claim: In 2,926 repositories, 4,860 context files were found across 2,634 repositories: CLAUDE.md 34.2%, AGENTS.md 32.3%, copilot-instructions.md 27.7%, GEMINI.md 3.3%; most repositories had one or two context files.
claims.quote: We identified 4,860 Context Files across 2,634 of the 2,926 repositories
claims.caveat: Figures are from the first version (v1). Later versions changed them (v5: 4,768 files in 2,586 of 2,853 repositories, CLAUDE.md 34.4%) and retitled the paper; a short companion paper was published at AIware 2026. Sample is repositories that use at least one agent tool, so adoption rates do not generalise to all repositories. Descriptive.

claims.claim: 518 pairs of context files reference each other instead of repeating content, most often CLAUDE.md pointing to another file (357 outgoing) and AGENTS.md being pointed to (368 incoming).
claims.quote: We found 518 file pairs that reference each other.
claims.caveat: Figures are from the first version (v1); in v5 the counts are 344 outgoing references from CLAUDE.md and 353 incoming to AGENTS.md, and the 518-pair total does not appear. Descriptive: shows files referencing each other, not whether that helps agents.

claims.claim: Codex builds its instructions by walking from the project root down to the working directory, reading at most one file per directory (AGENTS.override.md, then AGENTS.md, then configured fallback names), concatenating them root-first so files nearer the working directory come later and override earlier ones.
claims.quote: Codex concatenates files from the root down, joining them with blank lines.
claims.locator: Section 'How Codex discovers guidance' (Global scope, Project scope, Merge order)
claims.caveat: Documents Codex behaviour at the fetch date only; a global ~/.codex file is read first. Does not show how well the model follows the combined text.

claims.claim: Codex stops adding instruction files once their combined size reaches project_doc_max_bytes, which defaults to 32 KiB; the docs advise raising the limit or splitting guidance across nested directories if instructions are truncated.
claims.quote: stops adding files once the combined size reaches the limit defined by project_doc_max_bytes
claims.locator: 'How Codex discovers guidance' (Merge order) and 'Troubleshoot discovery issues' (Instructions truncated)
claims.caveat: Applies to Codex only; the limit is configurable in config.toml and the default may change.

claims.claim: GitHub Copilot reads repository-wide instructions from .github/copilot-instructions.md and path-specific instructions from .github/instructions/NAME.instructions.md files whose frontmatter sets applyTo; when both match, instructions from both files are used.
claims.quote: then the instructions from both files are used
claims.locator: Sections on repository-wide and path-specific instructions
claims.caveat: Documents Copilot behaviour at the fetch date; support differs between Copilot surfaces such as code review and the cloud agent (excludeAgent option).

claims.claim: For Copilot Chat on GitHub.com, all relevant instruction sets are provided together, with precedence from highest to lowest: personal instructions, then repository instructions (path-specific, repository-wide, agent instructions such as AGENTS.md), then organization instructions.
claims.quote: all relevant instructions are provided to Copilot
claims.caveat: Precedence is stated only for Copilot Chat on GitHub.com; the page says most other surfaces (Copilot CLI, VS Code, Visual Studio) combine the applicable files without a defined precedence. All relevant instructions are provided together, so precedence matters only where they conflict.

claims.claim: Copilot supports one or more AGENTS.md files anywhere in a repository, and the nearest AGENTS.md in the directory tree takes precedence while it works.
claims.quote: the nearest AGENTS.md file in the directory tree will take precedence
claims.caveat: Documents the product at the fetch date; does not describe how conflicts between nested files are resolved beyond nearest-wins.

claims.claim: Gemini CLI loads GEMINI.md from a global file in the home directory, from workspace directories and their parents, and just in time from a directory and its ancestors, up to a trusted root, when a tool accesses a file there, concatenating all found files into every prompt.
claims.quote: concatenates the contents of all found files
claims.caveat: Documents Gemini CLI behaviour on the main branch at the fetch date; says nothing about model adherence.

claims.claim: Gemini CLI GEMINI.md files can import other files with @file.md syntax (relative or absolute paths), the context filename is configurable (for example to AGENTS.md), and /memory reload re-scans all context files.
claims.quote: importing content from other files using the @file.md syntax
claims.locator: Sections: Modularize context with imports; Manage context with /memory
claims.caveat: Documentation of one tool at the fetch date only.

claims.claim: A documentation-consistency checker flagged at least one stale code reference (present at the file's first commit, gone at HEAD) in 82 of 356 sampled repositories (23.0%) and 230 of 18,048 verified references (1.27%); in a 50-hit manual check by one author, 64% were genuine and 36% false positive or ambiguous.
claims.quote: identifies stale code element references in 23.0% of repositories
claims.caveat: Authors call 23.0% a feasibility signal: the two-snapshot method misses later-added references, and 36% of sampled hits were false positives or ambiguous. One annotator. Measures references to code elements only, not wrong instructions, and not effect on agent behaviour.

claims.claim: One developer maintaining specification documents for a 108,000-line C# project reported about 1 to 2 hours per week of upkeep and at least two cases where outdated documents led an agent to write code conflicting with recent refactors; a session-start hook warns when source changes lack matching spec updates.
claims.quote: Specification staleness was the primary failure mode.
claims.caveat: Single developer, single project, no controlled comparison; the author notes team settings were not evaluated.

claims.claim: In 288 evaluated runs (15 tasks for Claude Code and 17 for Codex, from 3 repositories, 3 repeats each), giving the agent no context against the full AGENTS.md in every system prompt did not significantly change pass rates for Claude Code (53.3% vs 55.6%) or Codex (58.8% vs 56.9%).
claims.quote: Neither agent shows a statistically significant strategy effect.
claims.caveat: Small single-author preprint. The result is a bounded null: equivalence tests exclude effects larger than about 10 points for Claude Code and 15 for Codex, not smaller ones. Many tasks sit at floor or ceiling, so the omnibus test has low power (the author's own note); three repositories, two agents, one model each; gold-test pass or fail only.

claims.claim: On LongSWE-Bench, Claude 3.5 Sonnet solved 29% of issues at the 32K context bracket and 3% at 256K, with 100 instances per bracket.
claims.quote: long-context remains a weakness for all models
claims.caveat: Published at COLM 2025 (per the header of the arXiv PDF, v3); models are 2024-25 generation; the prompt holds the files from the fixing pull request plus randomly sampled files from the repository up to the bracket length, so this measures long-context prompting with distractor files, not an agent that fetches files; Claude 3.5 Sonnet has no result at 512K or 1M.

claims.claim: On LongCodeQA, the authors report that Gemini 2 Flash, Gemini 1.5 Pro and Gemini 2.5 Pro stayed between 63% and 72% up to 1M tokens (their Table 3 runs from 63.1% to 75.2%), while Qwen2.5-14B rose to 70.2% at 512K and fell to 40.0% at 1M.
claims.quote: neither monotonic nor uniform
claims.caveat: Multiple-choice question answering, not code editing; four options so chance is 25%; model-dependent, so it does not show a general decline with length.

claims.claim: Claude 3.5 Sonnet with a RAG pipeline solved 23, 23, 22, 21, 16 and 22 percent of LongSWE-Bench issues across the 32K to 1M brackets, against 29% falling to 3% at 256K without it.
claims.quote: RAG helps Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieve positive scores on LongSWE-Bench
claims.caveat: One model and one retrieval setup that the authors call a narrow view of RAG; retrieval pipeline, not an agent choosing what to read.

claims.claim: On LongCodeQA the same RAG setup for Claude 3.5 Sonnet scored 12.77 to 31.18 percent across brackets, which the authors describe as comparable to random guessing.
claims.quote: RAG negatively impacts the performance of Claude 3.5 Sonnet
claims.caveat: One model, one retrieval setup; four-option multiple choice; the authors attribute it to sensitivity of RAG to the task.

claims.claim: On Python LongCodeBench question answering, accuracy with answer options ranged from about 62% to 81% across models and context lengths, and fell to about 33% to 54% when the options were removed.
claims.quote: performance drops sharply when answer options are removed
claims.caveat: Preprint marked 'Work in Progress' in its arXiv comments; question answering rather than code editing; Python set only; it extends LongCodeBench and does not refute its context-length result.

claims.claim: Across 857 Claude Code sessions from one user (54,170 API calls, 4.45 billion effective input tokens), 21.8% of input tokens were structural waste: unused tool schemas 11.0%, stale tool results 8.7% and duplicated content 2.2%.
claims.quote: 21.8% of tokens are structural waste
claims.caveat: Single user over about four months, 15 projects, one agent product; of the 857 sessions only 59 are main (human-facing) sessions, the rest are 567 subagent, 154 compaction and 21 prompt-suggestion sessions; preprint; waste is defined by the author's taxonomy and says nothing about task success. The paper's Table 6 labels the 8.7% line 'static re-send' while the contributions text calls it stale tool results.

claims.claim: In a 681-turn live Claude Code session, evicting stale tool results shrank context from 5,038KB to 339KB, but the model re-requested 659 of 680 evicted items (97%) and the session ended on an API rate limit.
claims.quote: The 97% fault rate is a pathology, not a feature.
claims.caveat: One session by the author's own tool; the eviction policy was a simple age rule; the standardized-task comparison used a few API calls per condition, and compact-plus-trim cut effective input tokens 37.1% there.

claims.claim: In a 20-book library, a Codex agent navigating raw documents scored about 0.26 on English open QA, while the same agent with a flat progressive-disclosure skill pack scored about 0.46.
claims.quote: buys context, not intelligence
claims.caveat: Long-document QA on InfiniteBench, not code; preprint; the 0.26 versus 0.46 cell is one harness and model (Codex, gpt-5.4-mini) on English open QA at K=20 books; the paper's Table 2 shows the skill pack neutral or negative on Zh.QA and indistinguishable on En.MC, and Table 2 uses means over bundles and seeds with standard errors; a memorized-novel confound affects En.MC.

claims.claim: On a single book, a flat skill pack matched or beat raw-document navigation under the Pi and Claude-Code harnesses but added nothing under Codex, whose model already searches for the entities each question names.
claims.quote: adds nothing under Codex
claims.caveat: Long-document QA, not code; three harnesses and three models; preprint; gain depends on the harness.

claims.claim: In single-book tests a second, hierarchical routing level never beat the flat one-level pack and, on Pi with gpt-5.4-mini, cut English multiple-choice accuracy from 0.9126 to 0.6398; the authors attribute this to always-loaded child descriptions filling the router's context. At library scale the two were mixed.
claims.quote: A second, deeper routing level never helps
claims.caveat: Long-document QA, not code, and 'hierarchy' here means child skills with always-loaded descriptions, not a plan file pointing to step files; preprint.

claims.claim: In a preregistered test on a 709-page LLM-maintained wiki (40 questions, 960 runs), the progressive-disclosure retrofit cut cost per answer by 30% when reads were enforced, 34% when free and 58% when the old index was force-loaded, and answers cited 4.22 pages instead of 6.10.
claims.quote: Cost fell clearly in every condition we tested
claims.locator: Abstract; Section 5.2 Table 2 and Figure 3 (cost); Section 5.4 (pages cited)
claims.caveat: Knowledge-base question answering, not code; single author; one answering model (Claude Opus 4.8); the cost contrasts are retrofit arm A3 versus original A0 only; in the forced condition A0 preloads the 150 KB index while A3 gets only a keyword-retrieval result, so the 58% mostly reflects that difference; the paper captured no per-read telemetry, so the 'targeted access' mechanism is inferred (pages cited, tool turns); v2 revised in Oct 2026.

claims.claim: A capable tool-using agent given file-read and search tools never loaded the roughly 150 KB monolithic index in the pilot; it inferred the page path from the question and read the page directly.
claims.quote: A capable agent never loaded the large index at all.
claims.caveat: Pilot observation on one corpus and one model; wiki of 709 pages with descriptive paths; not code.

claims.claim: Answer quality from the retrofitted wiki was statistically non-inferior to the original (difference +0.01, 95% CI -0.27 to +0.26, margin 0.5), but non-inferiority was not shown when the catalog was force-loaded first.
claims.quote: Answers from the retrofitted knowledge base were as good as answers from the original
claims.caveat: Judge-model grading; the preregistered human-judge agreement gate failed, so the result rests on the model judge with sensitivity checks; not code.

claims.claim: Anthropic states that loading 50+ MCP tool definitions upfront takes about 72K tokens, for about 77K total context consumption before work begins, against about 8.7K total with a Tool Search Tool that discovers three to five tools on demand.
claims.quote: Total context consumption: ~8.7K tokens, preserving 95% of context window
claims.caveat: Vendor post describing an illustrative scenario, not a measured benchmark; method not given.

claims.claim: In Anthropic's internal MCP evaluations with large tool libraries, Opus 4 accuracy rose from 49% to 74% and Opus 4.5 from 79.5% to 88.1% with Tool Search Tool enabled.
claims.quote: Opus 4 improved from 49% to 74%
claims.caveat: Vendor-run internal eval with no sample size or task description; tool selection, not coding.

claims.claim: METR measured a 50% task-completion time horizon of about 110 minutes for o3 on tasks timed with human experts, and found the horizon of frontier models doubled roughly every seven months since 2019.
claims.quote: doubled approximately every seven months since 2019
claims.caveat: Preprint (arXiv v4, July 2026; no venue stated); mostly software and ML-research tasks with automatic scoring, which the authors say do not perfectly represent real intellectual work; tasks are timed by human baseliners; the authors note o3 lies above the long-run trend (p = 0.006) and the trend may have accelerated since 2024.

claims.claim: Across all models, success rate fell with human completion time, an exponential fit with R-squared of about 0.80 against log human time, and 80% time horizons were 4 to 6 times shorter than 50% horizons.
claims.quote: 80% time horizons are 4-6x shorter
claims.caveat: Same task suite and external-validity limits as R206; success is per-task pass/fail with 8 runs per pair; short tasks include 66 newly written ones.

claims.claim: In SWE-bench Verified, annotators estimated that fewer than 10% of issues take an experienced engineer more than an hour, and the released annotations define an easy subset of 196 tasks under 15 minutes and a hard subset of 45 tasks over one hour.
claims.quote: fewer than 10% of issues estimated to take longer than an hour
claims.locator: Section 'How difficult are the tasks?' and Distribution of difficulty labels
claims.caveat: Vendor post (OpenAI, updated Feb 2025; read from an Internet Archive copy because openai.com returns 403); estimates are annotator judgments of how long an experienced engineer who has had a few hours to learn the codebase would take, ensembled by majority or median, and the post says they may overestimate difficulty for a model that memorized the code; the 'fewer than 10%' sentence covers both SWE-bench Lite and Verified; per-bucket resolve rates are charts only.

claims.claim: ACON, which learns compression guidelines for observations and history from agent failures, cut peak tokens by 26 to 54 percent on AppWorld, OfficeBench and multi-objective QA while improving task success over other compression baselines.
claims.quote: reduces peak token usage by 26–54% while improving task success
claims.caveat: Peer-reviewed (ICML 2026) but not coding tasks; the compressor needs a failure-analysis optimization loop; success is relative to other compressors, not to no compression on every benchmark.

claims.claim: On SWE-bench Verified with Mini SWE Agent, adding SWE-Pruner cut token use by 23.1% with Claude Sonnet 4.5 and 38.3% with GLM 4.6, while resolve rate went from 70.6% to 72.0% and from 55.4% to 56.6%.
claims.quote: reduces token consumption by 23–38% while improving success rates
claims.caveat: Preprint; one agent scaffold (Mini SWE Agent), two models, 500 tasks, one count per cell with no variance reported (1.2 to 1.4 point gains are 6 to 7 more tasks solved, likely within noise); Python repositories only; needs a trained 0.6B pruning model.

claims.claim: When a successor coding agent took over an interrupted SWE-bench Verified task, giving it the predecessor's trace or notes cut median agent events by 20 to 59 percent and cumulative prompt tokens by 42 to 63 percent compared with repository state alone (181 handoff points, three open-weight successor models).
claims.quote: context helps effort more than final resolution
claims.caveat: Preprint; open-weight successors served locally (Qwen3.6-27B, Gemma-4-31B, Devstral-Small-2); 181 handoff points derived from only 75 SWE-bench Verified tasks; one OpenHands-style runtime; each handoff point evaluated once per view in the main study (a 3-attempt check on 40 points is reported); main-study predecessor is a single Qwen model; 'structured notes' are generated templates, not a persistent progress file maintained across sessions.

claims.claim: In the same takeover study, a raw trace raised solved rate by 6.1 to 14.9 points for all three successors, while note-based handoffs raised it significantly only for Devstral (+9.4 to +10.5 points) and not significantly for Qwen or Gemma.
claims.quote: note-based gains for Devstral are significant
claims.caveat: Same limits as R210; the authors call solved-rate gains supporting evidence; a raw trace is the heaviest handoff view, so this does not favor summaries.

claims.claim: LongHorizon-Harness, which has a manager hold task state, a fresh-context executor do each subtask and a read-only auditor check results, raised Qwen 3.7-Plus (with Claude Code as the backend) from 51.8% to 80.7% on WeaveBench and from 69.7% to 77.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, using 24% fewer tokens on Terminal-Bench 2.1 but 2.3 times more on WeaveBench.
claims.quote: Audit reports are the only cross-round memory
claims.caveat: Authors' own system, preprint; manager, fresh context and auditor are bundled, so it does not isolate fresh sessions from one long session; WeaveBench is not purely coding. With a stronger model on WeaveBench Games, the harness lowered scores on several tasks the baseline already solved.

claims.claim: With GPT-4 Turbo, rerunning the problems that failed from the problem statement alone with the benchmark's public tests added brought the cumulative share solved from 69.67% to 82.45% on MBPP (399 tasks), from 78.66% to 87.81% on HumanEval (164) and from 23.00% to 26.09% on 1,100 CodeChef problems, checked against all tests including those not shown to the model.
claims.quote: the more exhaustive the test suites are, the better the results tend to be
claims.caveat: Tests were the datasets' own human-written public tests, not tests the model wrote. Function-level (MBPP, HumanEval) plus whole-program CodeChef problems, not repository work. One main model (GPT-4 Turbo v1106, 2024), temperature 0, one seed. Problems were retried with tests only after failing without them, so there is no independent no-tests arm; a failure-feedback loop is a further stage reported separately. The paper header names the 39th IEEE/ACM ASE conference (Oct 2024).

claims.claim: With GPT-4-32k on MBPP, pass@1 was 67.13% with no tests in the prompt, 78.26% with one test and 80.88% with all validation tests; one simulated round of user-approved test feedback (TiCoder-PassFail) reached 81.56%.
claims.quote: adding tests in the prompt does help improve model performance
claims.locator: Section VIII-C, Tables IV and V
claims.caveat: Function-level benchmark, one model for this comparison. Test feedback is simulated with the dataset's reference tests as an idealized user, which the authors call an upper bound. Tests were dataset tests, not model-written. Venue not confirmed on the page.

claims.claim: In a 15-participant study where users judged AI code suggestions, mean task correctness was 0.40 with no test help, 0.84 with a pass/fail test-labelling assistant (p = 0.001) and 0.64 with a variant where users also supplied outputs (not significant); mean cognitive load was 45.46 versus 28.00 and 29.52.
claims.caveat: 15 participants, three short function-level tasks, 15-minute limit each. The task was picking the correct suggestion from five, not writing code with an agent. The time difference was not significant.

claims.claim: On 1,000 web-app tasks where the tests are the only prompt, pass@1 ranged from 0.952 (o1-preview) and 0.881 (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) down to 0.068 (Llama 3 8B) across 19 models.
claims.quote: tests are both prompt and verification
claims.caveat: Single-author preprint. It has no prose-prompt arm, so it does not show that tests-first helps, only that models can code from tests; its only comparison (a 'TLD' experiment, Table 8) edits the tests to fit the model's output and is not a prose-prompt control. Tasks are small React-style web features with the same tests used to prompt and to score, so passing the visible tests is the whole criterion. Reasoning models were run once, others up to ten times.

claims.claim: On SWT-Bench-Lite (276 issues), the best single-run issue-reproduction test writer, SWE-Agent told to run its own tests (SWE-Agent+), produced a fail-to-pass test for 19.2% of issues (18.5% successful), and general code agents matched dedicated test-generation methods.
claims.quote: general-purpose Code Agents already perform as well as domain-specific test generation methods
claims.caveat: GPT-4-class models (2024). Writing a valid reproduction test is hard: roughly four in five issues got none. Peer review (NeurIPS 2024 per brief) not shown on the page.

claims.claim: Keeping only the SWE-Agent patches on which all agent-generated tests passed raised the precision of its fixes to 47.8% at about 20% recall, which the authors describe as more than doubling it.
claims.quote: this more than doubles the precision of SWE-Agent
claims.locator: Section 5.3, Filtering Code Fixes with Generated Tests
claims.caveat: Precision gain comes with about 80% of correct fixes discarded (20% recall). SWE-Bench-Lite and 2024 models. The paper gives no measured unfiltered precision for SWE-Agent; it says only that state-of-the-art methods resolve around 20% of SWE-Bench-Lite, and that filtering 'more than doubles' precision to 47.8%.

claims.claim: Which SWT-Bench issues an agent solved (wrote a valid test) and which SWE-Bench issues it solved (fixed) overlapped little: SWE-Agent solved 44 and 50 with an overlap of 7, with no statistical evidence of correlation.
claims.quote: no statistical evidence of correlation
claims.caveat: Small counts; the test of independence assumes uniform hardness, which the authors note. Shows writing the test and writing the fix were not the same issues, not that tests are useless.

claims.claim: On 449 real issues from 12 Python repositories, GPT-4o given the issue and pre-fix code produced a fail-to-pass test for 84 issues zero-shot (tddScore 17.2) and 106 with the Auto-TDD pipeline (tddScore 22.6); Llama-3.1 got worse with Auto-TDD (51 to 37).
claims.caveat: Measures only whether a test fails before and passes after the real fix; it does not measure whether the tests help an agent fix the issue. One test file per issue, 12 repositories, three models (2024). Not peer reviewed as far as the page shows.

claims.claim: Showing the model the actual fix diff (write-code-first, test-later) barely changed results: Auto-TDD with GPT-4o produced 109 fail-to-pass tests versus 106 without the diff, and tddScore 23.6 versus 22.6.
claims.caveat: Compares what the test writer sees, not a full test-first versus test-after development workflow. Same benchmark limits as the row above. The authors call the difference not surprising.

claims.claim: On TDD-Bench-Verified (449 issues), GPT-4o wrote fail-to-pass tests for 84 issues zero-shot (18.7%), 141 with Otter (31.4%) and 166 with the five-test Otter++ ensemble (37.0%).
claims.caveat: Preprint; one test file per issue; 12 Python repositories. Ensemble of five heterogeneous prompts costs more. Test quality judged by fail-before/pass-after on the real fix.

claims.claim: Discarding a patch when all five Otter++ tests fail on it raised precision for the top 22 SWE-bench Verified leaderboard systems to 65-92% at 30-41% recall, except for one system whose precision rose by 22% to 167%; for the system ranked third, precision rose from 60.8% to 91.9% at 33% recall.
claims.quote: filtering by the generated tests boosts precision from 60.8% to 91.9%
claims.caveat: Trades recall for precision: most correct patches are also dropped. Leaderboard systems and models are 2024-25 vintage. Preprint.

claims.claim: Using the generated tests with CodeT-style ranking to pick among candidates from the top three leaderboard systems gave about a 2% improvement.
claims.caveat: A single sentence in the paper, without a table; the authors note these systems already used rankers and stronger models.

claims.claim: Ranking sampled solutions by agreement with model-generated tests (CodeT) raised code-davinci-002 pass@1 from 47.0% to 65.8% on HumanEval and from 58.1% to 67.7% on MBPP, and from 27.2% to 34.6% on APPS introductory problems.
claims.quote: absolute improvement of 18.8%
claims.caveat: Function-level and competitive-programming problems with 2022 Codex-family models; gains were small on harder problems (CodeContests 0.7% to 2.1%). Tests are model-written from the problem statement and can be wrong. Peer review (ICLR 2023 per brief) not shown on the page.

claims.claim: A multi-stage flow that iterates on public tests and then on AI-generated tests raised GPT-4 pass@5 on CodeContests from 19% to 44% on validation and from 12% to 29% on test, against a single direct prompt.
claims.quote: Iterating on public tests stabilizes and improves the solution
claims.caveat: The flow bundles many changes (reflection, YAML output, ranking, test iteration) and the paper has no ablation isolating generated tests, so the gain cannot be credited to tests. Competitive-programming problems, 2023-24 models, preprint.

claims.claim: When asked whether an assertion was correct, four LLMs were less accurate on correct assertions if the code under test was buggy than if it was correct, for example DeepSeek V3 55.17% vs 39.02% and GPT-4o-mini 60.33% vs 46.58% (full prompt).
claims.quote: predictions are derived towards the actual implementation
claims.caveat: Java, 24 repositories; buggy code made by mutation, so faults may differ from real ones. The task is classifying supplied assertions, not writing tests. Models are 2024-25. Peer review not confirmed.

claims.claim: Across 13 LLMs on Defects4J methods, prompting with buggy code produced on average 3.84% tests that passed the buggy code but failed the fixed one, versus 0.46% when given the fixed code, and effective bug-finding tests fell from 8.51% to 2.98%.
claims.quote: suppresses the generation of useful, bug-finding ones
claims.caveat: Java method-level unit tests, real bugs, tests written from the code under test (not from an issue). Defects4J may be in training data. Peer reviewed at ISSTA 2026.

claims.claim: In a benchmark of buggy student Python programs, 171 of 287 tests (59.6%) kept in CodiumAI CoverAgent's final suites and 62 of 91 (68.1%) in CoverUp's passed the buggy code but failed the reference solution, against 12 of 287 (4.2%) for unfiltered Copilot output.
claims.quote: tests that pass on buggy code but fail on correct implementations
claims.caveat: Student single-function programs from one course, three tools, one model setup; authors note it may not represent production bugs. Shows that a keep-only-passing-tests rule can lock in a bug, not that test-first fails. Preprint. Denominators as I recomputed them from Table I counts.

claims.claim: Across four models on SWE-bench Verified, prompts that flipped test writing for 37-75% of tasks produced no statistically significant change in resolution (exact McNemar, all p > 0.05), with 83.2% of tasks keeping the same outcome.
claims.quote: appears to be a weak lever for shifting task outcomes in this setting
claims.caveat: Agents wrote tests on their own as exploration; this is not test-first or TDD. Light mini-SWE-agent scaffold, 2025-26 models, prompt-only intervention. Suppressing tests cut cost with modest success drops. Preprint.

claims.claim: In agent-written tests on SWE-bench Verified from five models, value-revealing print statements outnumbered assertions for every model, and GPT-5.2 wrote new tests in 0.6% of tasks yet resolved 71.8% against 74.4% for Claude Opus 4.5.
claims.caveat: Observational comparison across models, not controlled; models differ in many ways other than test writing. Preprint.

claims.claim: On SWE-bench Verified (500 tasks), reproduction tests written by Agentless and SWE-Agent triggered the bug in 41-57% of tasks with a generated patch, and patches that passed the agent's own reproducer but failed the task were 4-5% of Agentless tasks and 18-30% of SWE-Agent tasks.
claims.quote: Trigger rates are 41–57%
claims.caveat: Two agents (Agentless, SWE-Agent), each with GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet (2024-era). Trigger and overfit rates are computed automatically from execution logs and marker strings over tasks with a generated patch, not by hand. Reproducers are written during repair, not before it. The paper header gives the ISSTA 2026 proceedings (PACMSE vol 3).

claims.claim: The Claude Code best-practices page shows a bug-fix prompt that asks for a failing test first: users report that login fails after session timeout, check the auth flow, write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix it.
claims.quote: write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix it
claims.locator: Provide specific context in your prompts (example prompt table)
claims.caveat: Documents a prompt example, not a measured effect. The page does not say tests must be committed first or must not be changed.

claims.claim: The Claude Code best-practices page suggests splitting test writing from implementation across sessions: one Claude writes tests, then another writes code to pass them.
claims.quote: have one Claude write tests, then another write code to pass them
claims.locator: Run multiple Claude sessions, Writer/Reviewer pattern
claims.caveat: Documents a suggested workflow in one sentence; no evidence is cited for it on the page.

claims.claim: Anthropic's prompting guide for Claude suggests that in the first context window the model writes tests in a structured file such as tests.json before starting work, and that the prompt reminds it that removing or editing tests is unacceptable.
claims.quote: It is unacceptable to remove or edit tests
claims.locator: Agentic systems, Long-horizon reasoning and state tracking, Workflows across multiple context windows
claims.caveat: Documents a recommended prompt, not a measured effect. It does not say tests are confirmed to fail before implementing.

claims.claim: Anthropic's prompting guide says Claude can sometimes focus too heavily on making tests pass at the expense of more general solutions, and gives a prompt asking for a general-purpose solution rather than workarounds.
claims.quote: focus too heavily on making tests pass at the expense of more general solutions
claims.locator: Agentic systems, Avoid focusing on passing tests and hardcoding
claims.caveat: Vendor statement with no rate or study cited; the mitigation prompt is not shown to work.
